title: Building py-kvcache: A Performance Characterization of External KV Caching for vLLM with NVMe SSDs (Joseph Kanichai, Tiziano De Matteis, Animesh Trivedi; Vrije Universiteit Amsterdam / IBM Research Zurich; cs.DC, 10 Sep 2026; work done Jan-Jul 2026; no venue)
id_read: arXiv 2609.11744v1 (PDF, full text via pdftotext, 108 kB)
setup: Models: Llama 3.2 3B Instruct (KV 114,688 B/token, 112 KiB) and Qwen3 4B Instruct 2507; batch: 50 concurrent requests in the disk-only test; docs 1k to 80k tokens; FP16 KV, one output token, 256-token KV blocks. Local node: Xeon Silver 4514Y, 256 GiB DDR5, 2x RTX 4000 Ada 20 GiB (PCIe 4.0), Kioxia CM7-R 1.92 TB (13.5 GB/s fio read), Samsung PM9A3 (6 GB/s). Snellius node: 2x EPYC 9334, 768 GiB, 4x H100 94 GiB (PCIe 5.0), Samsung PM1743 (13.5 GB/s). Baselines: LMCache disk backend, vLLM native KV Offload (DRAM + filesystem tier), GPU prefix cache only; vLLM v0.22, io_uring Python connector. Workloads: synthetic long-document, LongBench, SCBench, Alibaba Bailian traces.

numbers.what: Disk-only TTFT at 80k tokens, py-kvcache (with preload) vs LMCache
numbers.value: 2.0x faster (abstract); Fig 10a text: 2.0-2.5x across sizes; without preload about 1.5x

numbers.what: Preload contribution, py-kvcache with vs without preload
Tiered vs native vLLM KV Offload

numbers.value: 3.11x vs GPU prefix caching; 2.48x vs native CPU+disk offload; 1.26x vs LMCache
8k prompt needs 77.8% prefix reuse to break even; at 80k only 7.8%

numbers.what: Break-even storage bandwidth needed for a fully cached prompt
numbers.value: 23.2 GB/s at 1k tokens, 10.4 GB/s at 8k, 3.5 GB/s at 80k (KV 114,688 B/token)
Local RTX 4000 Ada: 1.12-1.79x vs GPU prefix caching, 1.10-1.25x vs LMCache. H100: TTFT identical to GPU prefix caching; avg request below 6,203-token SSD break-even for Qwen3 4B
fio 13.5 GB/s (CM7-R, PM1743), 6 GB/s (PM9A3); CPU-GPU copy 24-26 GB/s (local), 54-56 GB/s (Snellius)

catalog_numbers_correct.claim: Disk-loaded prefix KV does not always beat recompute; needs a load-vs-recompute decision
catalog_numbers_correct.true_value: Exactly the paper's thesis (abstract, Sec 5.2, Sec 7.4).

catalog_numbers_correct.claim: 'For our model, prefill is slow, so loading wins'
catalog_numbers_correct.true_value: Not in the paper; this is the catalog's own inference. The paper gives the criterion (required GB/s = KV bytes / prefill time). For our target the check is trivial: ~49 MB of KV (30B shape, 500 tokens) over a 19-22 s cold prefill needs about 2.5 MB/s, so loading wins by orders of magnitude (our arithmetic, not the paper's).

catalog_numbers_correct.claim: First-pass: 80k disk load 2.0x vs LMCache, preloading 1.34x, 1.23x tiered vs LMCache, within ~4% of native
catalog_numbers_correct.true_value: All four confirmed in the text; first pass was abstract-only and is correct.

why: The qualitative lesson transfers (admission test: load only if KV bytes / bandwidth < recompute time; for a 69 GB streamed model recompute of even 500 tokens costs 19-22 s so loading always wins). The numbers do not: all GPU servers (H100 / RTX 4000 Ada), vLLM, request-rate workloads, 3-4B dense models, 13.5 GB/s Gen5 SSDs, KV staged through host RAM to a GPU. No CPU-only, no MoE, no batch-1 laptop, no 8-32 GB RAM case.
quality_loss: None: exact KV reuse, FP16, no lossy step.
ablation: Yes: with/without preload (1.34x/1.66x), disk-only vs tiered, CPU tier adds 1.30x/1.18x/1.08x at 10k/40k/80k (Sec 7.3). Isolates scheduling/overlap, not relevant to a single-user cache.
limitations: Authors: two hardware classes, few models, FP16 KV only, one output token (no sustained-decode effect), single 256-token block size, no networked/RAID storage, CPU-staged I/O path only (GPUDirect could move the break-even), fast-moving vLLM/LMCache versions (Sec 10.1).
contradicts_our_findings: No. Consistent with Playbook/pubtech/D.md s2_3: our KV 98,304 B/token (30B shape) and 131,072 B/token (small MoE file) bracket the paper's 114,688 B/token for Llama 3.2 3B; load-vs-recompute arithmetic agrees.

title: On 10X Better Scalability: KV Stores Scale Up KV Cache [system SGLang-LSM] (Weiping Yu, Ye Jiarui, He Mengke, Junfeng Liu, Siqiang Luo; Nanyang Technological University; cs.DB, v2 25 Nov 2025; no venue shown)
setup: Server: Xeon 4314 (16 cores), 64 GB host RAM, NVIDIA A30 24 GB, 8 TB SSD, PCIe 4.0. Models GLM-4-8B (40 KB KV/token), GLM-4-32B (60 KB), Llama-3-8B (paper says 120 KB/token). Synthetic workload: 10 stages x 1000 requests, expected hit rates [0.2,0.3,0.5,0.7,0.5,0.3,0.1,0.3,0.5,0.7]; prompts 4k/8k/16k; warmup of 100 M tokens of KV written through. Baselines: SGLang(file) and SGLang(memory). Design: LSM-tree prefix index with key-value separation (tensor log), adaptive compaction. SSD bandwidth is not stated.

numbers.what: Absolute TTFT saving growing with prompt length

numbers.value: write anomalies / degraded reads at about 7 million files
0.81 s vs 0.85 s mean TTFT (GLM-9B 8k), up to 14% in write-heavy phases

catalog_numbers_correct.claim: up to 143% more hits
catalog_numbers_correct.true_value: 45.4% vs 18.7% at 4k prompts (+143%, comparing against the file backend, not against no cache).

catalog_numbers_correct.claim: 24% lower TTFT
catalog_numbers_correct.true_value: 16k prompts, GLM-4-8B: 1.78 vs 2.35 s; other cases 13-24%.

catalog_numbers_correct.claim: per-token KV for Llama3-8B is about 120 KB
catalog_numbers_correct.true_value: The paper says 120 KB; exact value from the architecture (32 layers x 2 x 8 KV heads x 128 x 2 B, from memory of the Llama-3-8B config) is 131,072 B, so the paper rounds down by about 8%. Our own measured small-MoE GGUF cache (131,072 B/token) equals the exact figure.

why: Value is an index/storage layout for millions of cached prefixes in a multi-tenant server (hit-rate under file-count limits). A single-user laptop holds a handful of sessions; the 7-million-file bottleneck, LSM compaction and A30 server setting do not exist there. Gain is over another disk cache, not over recompute.
ablation: Dynamic compaction on/off only (5% mean). No ablation of LSM vs layout vs cache size.
limitations: Authors note write throughput is bounded by the inference engine's own latency; benefits shrink for models with large per-token KV (Llama-3) because the reuse-vs-recompute cost gap narrows (Sec 4.3). Synthetic workload only.
contradicts_our_findings: No. Supports pubtech D.md note that KV/token is 98-131 KB; the 'KV bytes vs recompute' effect (smaller gain for larger KV) is the same break-even logic as P-0153.

title: ProMoE: Fast MoE-based LLM Serving using Proactive Caching (Xiaoniu Song, Zihang Zhong, Rong Chen, Haibo Chen; Shanghai Jiao Tong University / CAS key lab / Zhejiang University; cs.DC; v1 29 Oct 2024, v3 1 Sep 2025; no venue in the PDF)
setup: Models (Table 1): Deepseek-moe DS-1 16.4B/2.8B active, 28 layers, 64 experts, top-6; DeepSeek-V2-Lite DS-2 15.7B/2.7B, 27 layers, 64, top-6; Qwen1.5-moe QW-1 14.3B/2.7B, 24 layers, 60, top-4 (all FP16); Qwen2-moe QW-2 57.4B/14.2B, 28 layers, 64, top-8 (INT4); Mixtral-8x7B 46.7B/12.9B, 32 layers, 8, top-2 (INT4). Hardware: i9-14900K, 128 GB host DRAM, RTX 4090 24 GB, PCIe 4.0 (32 GB/s nominal, 23.9 GB/s measured); experts live in host DRAM and are copied to the GPU; attention/non-expert weights on GPU. Batch 1 default (1 to 4 swept), ShareGPT prompts. Frameworks: HF transformers and llama.cpp, both patched; 6,600 lines C++. Baselines: TO (transformers offload), LO (llama.cpp layer offload with CPU compute), UM (unified memory), static cache, LRU cache. Cache rate is a free parameter (50% of experts in the motivating examples). Predictor: per-layer MLP ~2M params, trained offline 1-2 h on one GPU from traces (90/10 split), runs on CPU in ~200 us; stride prefetching (prediction distance +1 layer, accuracy drops only 5%).

1.49x (up to 1.79x) vs static; 1.09x (up to 1.17x) vs LRU; 1.66x (up to 2.07x) vs all baselines incl. LO

numbers.value: learned 84.7% average (DS-1 and QW-2); token-ID based predictor 58.3%; skip-based 66.9% on QW-2
LO baseline faster than ProMoE in decode (25% of experts active)

numbers.value: 2.06x at INT4 falling to 1.105x at FP16

catalog_numbers_correct.claim: 'Decode speedup averages 2.07x (up to 5.02x) on transformers'
catalog_numbers_correct.true_value: 2.07x / 5.02x is the abstract's pooled decode figure across transformers and llama.cpp vs offloading baselines. transformers alone: 2.47x avg (up to 5.02x) vs TO/UM, 1.47x vs static, 1.31x vs LRU.

catalog_numbers_correct.claim: 'and 1.66x on llama.cpp'
catalog_numbers_correct.true_value: 1.66x (up to 2.07x) is true but is an average against all baselines including LO (CPU-compute offload) and static; against LRU it is only 1.09x (max 1.17x) and 1.14x in the cache-rate sweep.

catalog_numbers_correct.claim: First-pass: 'catalog's 1.66x/2.07x labels are swapped relative to text vs abstract'
catalog_numbers_correct.true_value: Not swapped: 2.07x is the abstract's pooled average, and 2.07x also happens to be the 'up to' of the llama.cpp 1.66x. Neither is a transformers-only average.

catalog_numbers_correct.claim: First-pass: predictor 84.7% (token-based 58.3%), lossless, llama.cpp 1.09x vs LRU / 1.49x vs static
catalog_numbers_correct.true_value: All confirmed in text.

why: Breaks: (1) GPU: experts move host DRAM -> 24 GB GPU over PCIe at ~24 GB/s with compute on a 4090, ours is CPU compute with NVMe at ~3 GB/s; (2) cache is 10-70% of experts in GPU memory (50% in the examples) while ours is 2-8 footprints of a 69 GB model; (3) trained per-layer MLP predictors on layer inputs (needs the model, 1-2 h training); (4) models are 14-57B with 64 experts, top-4..8, not 512 experts top-10; (5) the 1.66x/2.07x are averages against weak baselines (LO, static, TO, UM). Vs the only realistic baseline (LRU) in llama.cpp the decode gain is 1.09x.
quality_loss: None: lossless, computations identical to the original (Sec 8).
ablation: Yes (Fig 12/13): LRU base then +prefetch, +chunked prefetch, +early preemption, +reordered inference. In decode the stack gives 1.35x over LRU in transformers; in prefill naive prefetch alone gives little or negative and reordered inference gives most. Not a cache-vs-layout-vs-prefetch split in our terms.
limitations: Authors: Mixtral (25% expert activation) is better served by CPU compute (LO); low cache rates favour LO; improvement shrinks in llama.cpp because there is less overhead to hide; shrinks at FP16 (bigger experts, smaller cache rate).
contradicts_our_findings: No contradiction; mild support. Their token-ID-only predictor reaches 58.3% accuracy on 64 experts/top-6 (accuracy definition = share of predicted experts that are correct), comparable to our held-out id-based 0.31-0.43 precision on top-8-of-128. pubtech/D.md says 'ProMoE's 1.66x on llama.cpp ... rely on stronger predictors': more precisely 1.66x is an average dominated by LO/static baselines; vs LRU the full learned system gives 1.09x, close to our 1.00-1.075x.

title: HOBBIT: A Mixed Precision Expert Offloading System for Fast MoE Inference (Peng Tang*, Jiacheng Liu*, Xiaofeng Hou, Yifei Pu, Jing Wang, Pheng-Ann Heng, Chao Li, Minyi Guo; SJTU and CUHK; cs.LG; 6 Nov 2024; conference template 'Conference'17', no venue)
setup: Models: Mixtral-8x7B (45B total, 14B active, 32 layers, 8 experts, top-2, 87 GB fp16) and Phi-MoE (42B, 6.6B active, 32 layers, 16 experts, top-2). Hardware: RTX 4090 24 GB + 256 GB RAM + 64 cores, PCIe 4.0; NVIDIA Jetson AGX Orin 32 GB unified memory with 12 CPU cores; Samsung 980 PRO NVMe (7 GB/s nominal, about 3 GB/s in practice). Orin runs int8 models (int2 replacement experts), 4090 runs fp16 (int4 replacements). Batch 1; input/output lengths [16,32],[16,128],[128,32],[128,128]; 60 Alpaca samples. Built on llama.cpp (~8k lines). Baselines: Transformers, DeepSpeed-Inference, llama.cpp, MoE-Offloading, MoE-Infinity, Fiddler. Method: token-level dynamic loading (cache-miss expert of low importance is replaced by a low-precision copy), layer-level adaptive prefetching from gate input similarity, multidimensional cache policy (LRU+LFU+LHU+precision).

numbers.baseline: llama.cpp (mmap page faults on unified memory)

numbers.what: 4090 + CPU compute, decode vs llama.cpp / Fiddler
Ablation: adaptive prefetching alone (no precision substitution), decode
numbers.value: 1.01x Mixtral; slightly below 1.0x Phi-MoE; with dynamic loading about 1.05x; prefill about -10%
4.69-8.68% lower miss penalty vs LRU, 2.13-4.19% vs LFU

catalog_numbers_correct.claim: Up to 9.93x decode speedup
catalog_numbers_correct.true_value: 9.93x is Phi-MoE on Jetson Orin vs MoE-Infinity. Larger numbers exist in the paper: 13.0x and 18.9x vs llama.cpp on the same Orin (first pass missed these).

catalog_numbers_correct.claim: uses prefetch plus low-precision substitution for misses (lossy)
catalog_numbers_correct.true_value: Both present; quality change measured <=1% (GSM8K, TruthfulQA).

catalog_numbers_correct.claim: First-pass: 'accuracy drop <=1%'
catalog_numbers_correct.true_value: Table 3 confirms.

catalog_numbers_correct.claim: First-pass: 'next-layer top-1 prediction ~96% on Mixtral'
catalog_numbers_correct.true_value: Fig 7b; note this is top-1 of top-2-of-8.

catalog_numbers_correct.claim: Implicit: the 9.93x is mostly from prefetch
catalog_numbers_correct.true_value: Prefetch alone contributes 1.01x (Mixtral) to about 1.05x; the byte cut from int2/int4 substitution (1.19-1.57x alone) plus baseline weakness (MoE-Infinity and llama.cpp thrash on a 32 GB unified-memory board, 'severe page faults') produce the headline.

why: Closest regime of the rows read: llama.cpp base, batch 1, expert files on a ~3 GB/s NVMe, 32 GB board. Breaks: Orin has a GPU doing the compute (unified memory), model is top-2-of-8 (prediction/caching vastly easier than top-10-of-512), baselines are weak (llama.cpp with mmap thrash 13-19x slower), speedup comes from lossy precision substitution (needs low-precision copies of every expert stored too, +~25% storage for int2), the cache holds a large fraction of experts (Orin: 32 GB for an 87 GB int8-ish model).
quality_loss: Lossy: Table 3 GSM8K 0.52->0.51 (Mixtral fp16+int4), 0.83->0.82 (Phi-MoE); TruthfulQA truthful/informative within 0.02 (int8+int2 Mixtral: 0.50->0.52 truth, 0.91->0.90 info). Also Fig 3b: replacing <20% experts costs <=1%; skipping 10% costs >1% PPL.
ablation: Yes, all three parts separately (Sec 5.5). Key for us: prefetch alone 1.01x in decode, so the lossless prefetch part is about nothing, matching our 1.00-1.075x.
limitations: Authors focus on GPU-centric mode; CPU-assist mode benefits smaller (Sec 5.5); prefetch decode gain small due to misprediction penalty (Sec 3.3 / 5.5.2); highest speedup on slow-transfer devices.
contradicts_our_findings: No; strong support. HOBBIT's own prefetch ablation (1.01x / ~1.05x) is the lossless-prefetch number and agrees with our 1.00-1.075x. pubtech/D.md says 'HOBBIT's 9.93x rely on stronger predictors / lossy substitution': the paper shows the predictor contributes ~1.0-1.05x, so it is substitution plus weak baselines.

title: Budgeting Bytes: A Windowed Storage Roofline and Dual-Budget Architecture Ablations for Storage-Bound LLM Decoding (Hanhaodi Zhang, single author; cs.AR; 29 Jul 2026; 'draft for workshop submission')
setup: Part 1: sub-100M-parameter models (23 training runs, 3 scales) comparing address-determinism classes A0-A3. Part 2 (Sec 5.10): Qwen3-30B-A3B (48 layers, 128 experts, top-8; 4-bit 18 GB) on an 8 GB RK3588 ARM board with eMMC (277 MB/s sequential, 237 MB/s at 2.6 MB expert grain) and on an Apple M4 16 GB unified memory. Real prefetch advisor in llama.cpp: decode-time madvise(WILLNEED) over mmap'd expert ranges, driven by a learned per-layer predictor or captured routing. Single-run per configuration. A100 PCIe offload path used for the reconciliation (25.4 GB/s H2D).

catalog_numbers_correct.true_value: In Sec 5.8 'Artifact' and Sec 5.10: a decode-loop madvise(WILLNEED) advisor compiled into llama.cpp's common library, driven by a learned per-layer predictor (first pass could not verify; now verified).

catalog_numbers_correct.true_value: 18.8% is from the author's own trained 24M-parameter toy MoE (8 experts, top-2), not a published top-2-of-8 model like Mixtral. On the real Qwen3-30B-A3B the same previous-token policy gets 46.7% top-8 hit.

catalog_numbers_correct.claim: First-pass: 91.2% pre-attention probe; prefetch fails even with oracle; 22x by fitting
catalog_numbers_correct.true_value: All in the abstract and Sec 5.10. 22x is Q2_K on an M4 16 GB with Metal, quality unmeasured (Limitations).

catalog_numbers_correct.claim: First-pass: 'fitting the model gave 11.5 tok/s (22x)'
catalog_numbers_correct.true_value: 11.5/0.51 = 22.5x; note the baseline is the 0.51 tok/s ctx-2048 run.

why: Supports our regime directly: storage-bound, model larger than RAM (ϕ about 0.17 for the 8 GB board; ours 8/69 about 0.12), llama.cpp, mmap, madvise. Breaks: eMMC at 277 MB/s is about 11x slower than our 3 GB/s NVMe (the byte-volume wall is far lower), ARM board, 128 experts top-8 not 512/top-10, the 22x 'fit' lever uses a GPU-resident Q2_K that does not apply when the model is 69 GB.
quality_loss: Q2_K fit result: coherence checked, task quality not measured (authors, Limitations). Prefetch is lossless.
ablation: Yes, directly relevant: temporal prefetch vs oracle prefetch vs no prefetch vs blind readahead; layout headroom 1.24x. No cache-size sweep.
limitations: Single-run per configuration; sub-100M ablations; roofline compute model single-anchor calibrated; intermediate band (ϕ large but incomplete) argued from end points, not swept; Q2_K quality unmeasured; one A100 path and one edge board.
contradicts_our_findings: Consistent. Previous-token top-8 hit 46.7% on Qwen3-30B matches our persistence 0.42-0.46 (D.md). Their oracle-prefetch null at saturated bandwidth matches our 'shared disk is the bottleneck' reading (oracle 1.25-1.6x vs 1.9x bound) in direction; caution: our sim is not fully bandwidth-saturated at 3.1 GB/s (disk 188 ms vs compute 219 ms per token) so our oracle still shows 1.25-1.6x, while theirs is fully saturated (0.13 tok/s, 277 MB/s).

title: (a) Pre-Attention Expert Prediction and Prefetching for Mixture-of-Experts Large Language Models (Shien Zhu, Samuel Bohl, Robin Oester, Gustavo Alonso; ETH Zurich Systems Group; cs.CL; 10 Nov 2025; 'under review by a journal'). (b) Speculating Experts Accelerates Inference for Mixture-of-Experts (Vivan Madan*, Prajwal Singhania*, Abhinav Bhatele, Tom Goldstein, Ashwinee Panda; cs.LG; 9 Mar 2026)
id_read: arXiv 2511.10676v1 (full text, 57 kB) and arXiv 2603.19289v1 (full text, 43 kB)
setup: (a) Models: DeepSeek-V2-Lite (16.4B/2.4B active, 27 layers, 64 experts, top-6 + 2 shared), Qwen3-30B-A3B (30.5B/3.3B, 48 layers, 128 experts, top-8), Phi-mini-MoE (7.6B/2.4B, 32 layers, 16 experts, top-2). Per-layer 2-linear-layer predictors on the pre-attention (post-LayerNorm) activation of the same layer, trained on 10M MMLU-derived samples, 30 epochs, ranking-aware loss; predictors run on CPU in 0.075-0.129 ms while attention takes 0.73-1.13 ms. Hardware: TITAN RTX 24 GB, 128 GB RAM for accuracy; loading micro-benchmarks on V100-32GB / A100-40GB / A100-80GB (6 DeepSeek-V2-Lite experts = 99 MB). No end-to-end system. (b) Models Qwen3-30B-A3B, GLM-4.7-Flash, GPT-OSS-20B/120B, Qwen3-235B-A22B; A6000 48 GB with 128 GB DRAM over PCIe 4.0, A100 80 GB with 256 GB, GH200 96 GB with 480 GB over NVLink-C2C; batch 1, prompt 1k-64k, 32 output tokens; engine YALIS; expert weights pinned in CPU memory; GLM-4.7-Flash and GPT-OSS-120B speed runs use random expert weights.

catalog_numbers_correct.claim: Pre-attention routers reach 93-98% accuracy by predicting from hidden state
catalog_numbers_correct.true_value: Table 4 reports FIRST-LAYER accuracy; exact-match 93.03 / 94.69 / 97.62% (Arch 1). Arch 2 is 92.31 / 91.82 / 96.63%. Authors say other layers are similar or better, but only layer-1 numbers are tabulated.

catalog_numbers_correct.claim: (catalog) a much stronger predictor than the expert-id co-occurrence table used here (0.31-0.4x)
catalog_numbers_correct.true_value: Metrics differ: theirs is exact match of the whole expert set (which for top-8-of-128 is a hard criterion) from a trained per-layer net with MMLU-distribution training data on the same layer's pre-attention state, i.e. a 'no lead beyond attention time' predictor.

catalog_numbers_correct.claim: First-pass: 'no end-to-end speedup, estimated 0.27-0.64 ms/token saved'
catalog_numbers_correct.true_value: 0.27-0.64 ms/token is the expected REMAINING loading time (misprediction rate x load time); the saving versus Fate is up to 1.37 ms/token (Sec 6.2). No end-to-end measurement exists in paper (a).

catalog_numbers_correct.claim: First-pass: loading 6 experts 33.5-49.8 ms from disk vs 4.0-9.5 ms from memory
First-pass: (b) up to 14% TPOT reduction
catalog_numbers_correct.true_value: Qwen3-30B-A3B on A6000; 5-8% on other platforms. But the speculated experts are executed instead of the true ones (lossy for Qwen3, see Table 1).

why: (a) Prediction window is attention time of one layer (0.73-1.13 ms), a one-layer lead; no system. Models have 16-128 experts, top-2..8 and bf16; disk numbers are from V100/A100 hosts. (b) CPU-to-GPU PCIe/NVLink offload where compute is only 8-13% of TPOT, so the Eq. 1 bound caps the win at that fraction; it executes speculated rather than true experts (quality loss on Qwen3). Neither has NVMe-bound streaming, a 2-8-footprint cache or 512 experts. The pre-attention predictor accuracy (91-98%) is nevertheless a data point that same-layer routing is predictable at one-layer lead, which is the quantity our oracle sim (1.25x top-4 / 1.59x top-8) bounds.
quality_loss: (a) none (prediction only). (b) Router-PF: Qwen3-30B-A3B average 0.817 -> 0.641, GSM8k 0.950 -> 0.576; GPT-OSS models within ~2 pts; estimator variants recover to 0.75-0.77.
ablation: (a) loss-function and architecture comparison (Table 3), not a prefetch-vs-cache split. (b) Router-PF vs Est-PF vs Hybrid-PF (Table 1) and context-length sweep of compute vs copy (Fig 7/8).
limitations: (a) Authors list future work: end-to-end integration with caching, larger expert counts; accuracy given for layer 1. (b) bound min(copy, compute); gains shrink with fast links (5-8%); quality drops on Qwen3; no KV-cache offload support so contexts limited; random expert weights for two models.
contradicts_our_findings: No. (a) is consistent with D.md's 'Unmeasured: pre-attention predictors'; their disk-vs-memory table (5-8x) says nothing about NVMe on a Mac. (b)'s Eq. 1 (gain <= min(copy, compute)) is the same overlap bound as our ~1.9x/1.09x numbers; its measured 9-14% when compute is 8-13% of TPOT matches 'prefetch hides at most the compute share'.

title: Delta Decompression for MoE-based LLMs Compression [D2-MoE] (Hao Gu*, Wei Li*, Lujun Li*, Qiyuan Zhu, Mark Lee, Shengjie Sun, Wei Xue, Yike Guo; HKUST / Birmingham / others; cs.LG; 24 Feb 2025; ICML 2025 per proceedings listing (PDF itself shows no venue))
setup: Models: Mixtral-8x7B, DeepSeekMoE-16B-Base, Phi-3.5-MoE, Qwen2-57B-A14B. Training-free: Fisher-weighted merge of experts into a shared base, truncation-aware SVD of per-expert deltas, semi-dynamic structured pruning of the base. Calibration: 512 random WikiText-2 samples (compression time e.g. 19 min for the scale matrix on Mixtral). NVIDIA A100s. Evaluation: perplexity on WikiText-2/PTB/C4 and 7 zero-shot tasks. Throughput test: Mixtral-8x7B, batch size 64, compression 60/70/80%. Baselines: NAEE, MoE-I2, LoSparse, MC-SMoE, SparseGPT, ASVD.

numbers.value: WikiText-2 PPL Fisher 5.28 vs frequency 6.42, mean 7.66, TIES 12.45, RegMean 187

catalog_numbers_correct.claim: Shared base from Fisher-weighted merging plus SVD-compressed per-expert delta, pruning of the base
catalog_numbers_correct.true_value: Abstract and Sec 3.

catalog_numbers_correct.claim: 40-60% compression on Mixtral, Phi-3.5, DeepSeek and (Qwen2)
catalog_numbers_correct.true_value: Abstract: 40-60%; Table 2 also has 20%.

catalog_numbers_correct.claim: First-pass: Mixtral PPL 3.98 -> 4.65 / 5.28 / 6.46; avg acc 0.63 -> 0.60 / 0.57 / 0.52; throughput 277.7 vs NAEE 271.9 at batch 64
catalog_numbers_correct.true_value: All confirmed in Tables 2 and 4. 'No uncompressed throughput given' also confirmed.

catalog_numbers_correct.claim: Implicit: the speed gain is a decode speedup
catalog_numbers_correct.true_value: Throughput of 270-313 tok/s is at batch 64 on A100, compute-bound; the 'speed' reflects fewer FLOPs, not fewer streamed bytes.

why: Gains are model-size cuts of 20-80% by parameter dropping (lossy), measured on a GPU at batch 64. The shared-base idea is the one we want, but (i) quality: Mixtral at 40% already loses 0.06 average accuracy and +33% PPL, at 60% 0.11 and +62%; (ii) it reduces stored parameters, so bytes per streamed expert fall by at most 1/(1-ratio) (1.25-2.5x for 20-60%), consistent with our 1.3-2.5x closed-form; (iii) fp16 baseline (not 4.3 bpw), so the real byte saving vs a 4-bit model is not shown; (iv) base weights stay resident, delta SVD factors add compute; (v) no offloading experiment.
quality_loss: Yes, see numbers: Mixtral avg acc -0.03/-0.06/-0.11 at 20/40/60%; DeepSeekMoE-16B 60% avg acc 0.41 vs 0.56.
ablation: Yes: merge method (Table 5), base/delta compressors (Table 6), compression-ratio split between base and delta (Table 7), calibration data (Tables 8, 9). Not isolating bytes vs compute.
limitations: Authors: decomposition and pruning steps have some complexity (Limitations); no stated discussion of offloading.
contradicts_our_findings: No. Consistent with D.md s2_5 (published methods achieve 40-60% only with measurable loss). One caveat in D.md: it cites D2-MoE as 'consistent with needing fitted merging' for our OLMoE flat-spectrum probe; the paper provides no spectrum analysis of the delta, only the working-method results.

title: MoBE: Mixture-of-Basis-Experts for Compressing MoE-based LLMs (Xiaodong Chen, Mingming Ha, Zhenzhong Lan, Jing Zhang, Jianguo Li; Inclusion AI / Ant Group, Renmin University, Westlake University; cs.LG; 7 Aug 2025)
setup: Models: Ling-Lite-Chat, DeepSeek-V2-Lite-Chat, Qwen3-30B-A3B-2507, Qwen3-235B-A22B-2507, DeepSeek-V3-0324 (671B), Kimi-K2-Instruct (1T; 384 experts, trained in two groups of 64 bases). Each up/gate expert matrix W = A B with B re-parameterised as a SiLU/tanh of a linear combination of m basis matrices shared across the layer (m = 4 for the small models, 32 / 64 / 128 for large); down projections untouched; fit by Adam (lr 0.07) on reconstruction error, data-free (no calibration), on H100s; no distillation. Variant MoBE-dagger reduces active experts k->k' to hold active parameters constant. Baselines: D2-MoE (not run on the 3 largest models, too costly), MoLAE. Benchmarks: 15 (ARC-C, IFEval, GPQA, BBH, MMLU, CEval, CMMLU, Math, GSM8k, AIME24/25, MBPP, HumanEval, MultiPL-E, LCB).

numbers.value: authors: about 1.4% accuracy lost converting to MoBE, 0.5% for dagger
mean effective rank > 1593 in most layers, above the SVD break-even threshold 1593

catalog_numbers_correct.claim: Parameters cut 24-30% on Qwen3-235B, DeepSeek-V3 and Kimi-K2
1-2% accuracy drop
catalog_numbers_correct.true_value: Absolute drops on the three large models are 0.6 / 1.3 / 1.3 points (abstract: '1%-2%'); but Qwen3-30B-A3B at 24% loses 2.8 points and individual hard benchmarks lose 4-9 points (AIME, LCB, MultiPL-E).

catalog_numbers_correct.claim: First-pass: 'Qwen3-30B 24% -> 78.6 to 75.8'
catalog_numbers_correct.true_value: Confirmed.

catalog_numbers_correct.claim: First-pass: no speed numbers; needs custom kernel; extra active params
catalog_numbers_correct.true_value: Authors' Limitations; MoBE-dagger cuts k to compensate.

catalog_numbers_correct.claim: First-pass: only gate/up compressed; trained optimisation
catalog_numbers_correct.true_value: Sec 3; Adam fit of reconstruction error (data-free, not 'training' of the LLM).

why: Reduces total params 24-30% (1.3-1.4x bytes) at bf16 on H100; no streaming; extra per-expert factors can raise active parameters; quality cost 0.6-2.8 average points, much worse on hard reasoning. The useful finding for us is negative: shared basis matrices lose information because expert matrices have effective rank above the SVD break-even, i.e. independent experts, which matches our flat-spectrum probe.
quality_loss: Yes (Table 3): -0.6 to -2.8 average points; -4 to -9 on AIME/LCB/MultiPL-E for Qwen3-30B-A3B.
ablation: Yes: activation function (SiLU/tanh best, ReLU worse, Fig 6), Z-score normalisation (Fig 7). No cache/bytes ablation.
limitations: Authors: slight accuracy drop remains (suggest full-network KD); MoBE needs several fused-MoE kernel calls, so a dedicated mega-kernel is required to realise speed.
contradicts_our_findings: No. Supports pubtech/D.md: 24-30% cut (1.3-1.4x bytes) vs the 3.6x claimed by the family; effective-rank argument agrees with our OLMoE probe (16 of 64 components = 27.8% of centred energy vs 25% chance).

title: MoE-SVD: Structured Mixture-of-Experts LLMs Compression via Singular Value Decomposition (Wei Li*, Lujun Li*, Hao Gu, You-Liang Huang, Mark Lee, Shengjie Sun, Wei Xue, Yike Guo; PMLR 267 (ICML 2025), pp 35209-35230)
id_read: ICML 2025 camera-ready PDF (proceedings.mlr.press/v267/li25az; no arXiv id found), full text, 87 kB. First pass read only the poster abstract.
setup: Models: Mixtral-8x7B and 8x22B, Phi-3.5-MoE, DeepSeekMoE-16B, Qwen2. Training-free: sensitivity-based selective decomposition of expert layers, then one shared V matrix across all experts and top-k selected U matrices; optional LoRA fine-tune (MoE-SVD-dagger). Calibration 512 samples. Runtime = throughput on a single NVIDIA H800 (batch size and sequence length 32 mentioned for the speed figures). Baselines: ASVD, SVD-LLM, MoE-I2, MC-SMoE, MoE-Compression, Wanda/SparseGPT 2:4, LoSparse.

catalog_numbers_correct.claim: One V matrix shared across experts, U matrices trimmed
catalog_numbers_correct.true_value: Abstract/Sec 3.

catalog_numbers_correct.claim: 60% compression with faster inference
catalog_numbers_correct.true_value: Speedup at 60% is 1.78x on Mixtral and 1.51x on Phi-3.5 (abstract says 1.5x), but Mixtral at 60% has average accuracy 0.37 vs 0.63 and WikiText PPL 13.52 vs 3.98, so the abstract's 'minimal performance loss' does not hold at 60% in its own Table 2. The 1.2x speedup pairs with 20% compression (acc 0.58).

catalog_numbers_correct.claim: First-pass: 60% compression, 1.5x faster, training-free (abstract)
catalog_numbers_correct.true_value: Matches abstract; first-pass caveat 'hardware and tables unverified' now resolved: single H800.

why: GPU single-device throughput gain from fewer FLOPs/bytes of an in-memory model; the speedup (1.2-1.8x) comes with large quality loss at the ratios that give it. Streaming from NVMe would at best see the bytes ratio (60% cut = 2.65x fewer params by Table 11) but accuracy 0.37 is unusable. Shared V across experts is a different sharing axis (input-side) from the shared-basis-across-experts idea we tested, but gives no spectrum evidence either.
quality_loss: Yes (Table 2): Mixtral avg acc -0.05 at 20%, -0.13 at 40%, -0.26 at 60%; LoRA recovers only ~0.02 at 20%.
ablation: Yes (App B/C/D): selective decomposition, V sharing, top-k U, LoRA, significance test over 3 runs (Table 12). No bytes-vs-compute split.
limitations: Authors: SVD methods add communication overhead under tensor parallelism (Limitations; App B.4).
contradicts_our_findings: Corrects pubtech/D.md only in that the row is no longer 'unmeasured beyond the spectrum probe': the published Table 2 shows large losses at 50-60% compression. No conflict with our results.

title: Bandwidth-Efficient Adaptive Mixture-of-Experts via Low-Rank Compensation (Zhenyu Liu*, Yunzhen Liu*, Zehao Fan, Garrett Gagnon, Yayue Hou, Nan Wu, Yangwook Kang, Liu Liu; Rensselaer Polytechnic Institute, UMass Amherst, George Washington Univ., Samsung Semiconductor; arXiv Dec 2025 (v1 18 Dec 2025 per first pass); no venue in PDF)
setup: Models: Mixtral-8x7B (32 layers, 8 experts, top-2, 45.1B expert params), Mixtral-8x22B (56 layers, 8, top-2, 135.5B), DeepSeek-MoE-16B (28 layers, 64 experts, top-6 + 2 shared). Method: quantise all experts to INT2/INT3 (HQQ-style), precompute per-expert low-rank (SVD) compensators of the quantisation residual with kurtosis-guided rank allocation (average rank budget 32 Mixtral / 64 DeepSeek, quantised to INT3); at inference transfer low-bit experts plus compensators only for the top-n experts per token (n=1 for Mixtral, 3 for DeepSeek) and keep others low-bit. Evaluation: 7 zero-shot tasks + MMLU 5-shot + WikiText PPL; systems: H100 80 GB + DDR over PCIe (GPU-only offloading) and a simulated GPU+near-data-processing device (512 GB/s) using Ramulator and the MoNDE configuration. Input length 256, outputs 128/256/512; batch size not stated; whether the GPU-only throughput is measured or modelled is not stated. Profiling in Sec 2: Mixtral-Offloading on an H100 PCIe + EPYC 9334, FP16 experts, shows time dominated by host-device movement.

numbers.value: INT3 avg +0.45 pts, INT2 avg +8.24 pts (MMLU +1.11 / +10.50)

numbers.what: Restoring only top-1 expert at INT2, Mixtral-8x7B

numbers.value: rank 16 = 0.32 MB (0.75% of one INT2 expert); rank 128 = 2.53 MB (6.03%); PPL falls 7.05 -> 3.77 from rank 16 to 128 (Mixtral INT2 ablation)

catalog_numbers_correct.claim: For offloaded MoE, transfers dominate runtime
catalog_numbers_correct.true_value: Fig 1(a): host-device movement dominates (FP16 Mixtral-Offloading on H100).

catalog_numbers_correct.claim: A low-rank compensator offsets low-bit expert quantization error, so a low-bit base is streamed and a small correction (cut off)
catalog_numbers_correct.true_value: Per-expert compensator for the top-n router-ranked experts only (n=1 Mixtral, 3 DeepSeek); the other experts stay plain INT2/INT3.
All confirmed.

catalog_numbers_correct.claim: First-pass: 'batch size unspecified'
catalog_numbers_correct.true_value: Still not stated; only input/output lengths.

why: Relevant to our 'low-bit base + small residual for the few most important experts' (family 9), not to shared-basis (family 5): compensators are per-expert and the base is plain low-bit. The speedups (5-8x) are dominated by FP16 -> 2-3-bit byte reduction against an FP16 PCIe-offload baseline and a HOBBIT baseline; vs a 4-bit streamed baseline the byte gain would be ~1.3-2x. GPU/H100, 8-64 experts, top-2..6; performance partly simulated. Critically, the fine-grained model (DeepSeek-MoE-16B, 64 experts, top-6; closest to our 512/top-10) is NOT rescued: INT2 + top-3 compensation gives MMLU 28.75% (chance 25%) and PPL 10.99; the benefit relies on Mixtral's skewed router (top-1 dominates).
quality_loss: INT2 uniform: -21 to -36 pts average accuracy. With method: Mixtral-8x7B INT2 MMLU 47.53% (top-1 restored; FP16 reference MMLU not read in text, figure only); DeepSeek-MoE-16B INT2 MMLU 28.75%; INT3 within ~0.5-1.6 pts of HQQ INT3.
ablation: Yes (Fig 8, Table 2): number/position of restored experts, rank budget, kurtosis-guided vs uniform rank (PPL 7.05 vs 7.55 at rank 16). Isolates the compensation part, relevant to family 9.
limitations: Authors: DeepSeek needs higher-rank compensators or more restored experts (smaller gains); compensator transfer assumed negligible; future work on rank allocation and adaptive top-n.
contradicts_our_findings: No. Consistent with D.md s2_5 closed form (byte cut with overlap 1.0x at 16/32 GB) and relevant to F.md family 25 (2-bit base + refinement): evidence that a 2-bit base needs a skewed router to be recoverable. The 'shared basis' reading in the P07 first pass catalog row is right: this paper is per-expert.
